title: The Dow fell 444 on Wednesday. 91 paper puts on stocks that also fell were bought and sold that day, and 83 of them lost
author: QuanTradin
selftext:
Disclosure: I built the paper trading platform these bots run on. Fake money, real prices, nothing to sell here, no link.

Wednesday 9/30 the Dow fell 444 and SPY closed about half a percent down. If you'd asked me the night before what a red day does to long puts, I'd have said they're the one thing that should be fine. So I pulled every long put that closed on my platform that day, across all the paper accounts (11 of them held puts), and split them by what the underlying actually did.

| group | closed | won | P&L, paper | median put fill change | median stock move that day |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| stock fell, put bought AND sold Wed | 91 | 8 | -$37,886 | -6.2% | -1.0% |
| stock fell, put held from earlier | 24 | 4 | -$5,210 | -10.0% | -1.0% |
| stock went up (AAPL, ADBE among them) | 35 | 4 | -$34,802 | | up |
| all long puts | 150 | 16 | -$77,897 | | |

The bottom two rows don't surprise me. ADBE closed up almost 3% and AAPL closed up about 1% on a red index day, so puts on them losing is just the stock not doing what the index did. The index is not your underlying, and I keep relearning that.

The top row is the one I can't fully explain yet. 91 puts on stocks that fell about 1% that day, bought and sold inside the same session, and 83 of them lost. The median put was sold 6.2% below what it cost.

What I know about how the fills work, because I wrote that part: the desk buys at the ask and sells at the bid, never the middle. On a same-day round trip that's the whole spread paid in a few hours, and on cheaper strikes the spread is a big slice of the premium. So some of the -6.2% is just the price of getting in and out.

What I don't know yet is how much of it is timing. A lot of these rules fire on a move that has already happened, so the put gets bought after the stock already dropped, with the IV already up, and then the stock drifts sideways or bounces into the close. A 1% down day measured close to close can still be a losing day for a put bought at 11am. I haven't split entry time against the intraday low yet, which is the next thing I'm going to run.

What I'm fairly sure it isn't: a bug in direction. I checked the right column and the qty sign on all 150, they're all long puts, and the stocks-up rows lose the way you'd expect.

Two other things from the same day, so nobody thinks I'm cherry picking a bad bucket. Long calls that closed Wednesday: 278, 62 won, -$13,509 paper. Plain stock trades: 2,004 closed, roughly flat (+$1,931 paper). So it wasn't a bad day for the platform so much as a bad day to be buying premium in a hurry.

If you trade puts intraday on a red tape, how do you decide whether the move is already priced into the option by the time your rule says go. I'd like to know what people actually check before clicking buy.
